title: How do you calculate weighted averages quickly in a case interview?
description: Weighted averages explained with case examples: blended margins, average prices across segments, and how mix changes move the average.
hook: Weighted averages appear in many cases, often without being named: a blended margin across products, an average price across customer groups. Getting them wrong is one of the most common maths slips. Here is how to get them right quickly.
body:
The idea

An ordinary average treats every item equally. A weighted average gives each item a weight, usually its share of sales or volume.

A worked example: blended margin

A company sells two products. Product A: £60M of sales at a 10% margin. Product B: £40M at a 30% margin.

Wrong: (10% + 30%) ÷ 2 = 20%. Right: (60 × 10% + 40 × 30%) ÷ 100 = (6 + 12) ÷ 100 = 18%.

Mix changes

Next year sales shift to £80M of A and £20M of B, with the same margins. Blended margin: (8 + 6) ÷ 100 = 14%. Profit falls from £18M to £14M even though total sales are flat and neither product's margin changed. This is a mix effect, and it is often the hidden answer to a profitability case.

A quick method

  1. Multiply each value by its weight.
  2. Add them up.
  3. Divide by the total weight.

Practise

Try: 70% of customers pay £10 and 30% pay £20. Average price? (0.7 × 10 + 0.3 × 20 = 7 + 6 = £13.) More in the practice questions.

When the mix changes, the average moves even if nothing else does

Imagine a company selling premium and budget plans. It has 100 premium customers paying £40 a month and 400 budget customers paying £10. Total monthly revenue is 100 × £40 + 400 × £10 = £8,000 across 500 customers, so average revenue per customer is £16. A simple mean of £40 and £10 would give £25, which is wrong because the plans have different numbers of customers.

Now suppose both prices remain unchanged but the customer mix shifts to 250 premium and 250 budget customers. Total monthly revenue becomes £12,500, and the weighted average rises to £25. The business has improved its reported average without raising either price. That distinction matters in subscription pricing, hotel rates, airline yields and gross-margin analysis.

The method is always the same: multiply each group's value by its weight, sum the products and divide by the total weight. Check that the answer falls between the lowest and highest group values. If it falls outside, you have a calculation or unit error.

A useful case question is whether the higher average reflects genuine improvement or a mix shift. Separate within-segment changes from between-segment changes before recommending a new price strategy. In your recommendation, describe what caused the movement, not just that the headline average increased.
